conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood. 

The short questionnaire we’ll use is the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days—nothing more, nothing less. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless your safety is at immediate risk. My hope is that this gives us both a clearer picture of how to keep you feeling as steady and cared-for as possible.

We’ll take each question one at a time, and I’ll re-phrase them in everyday language so they feel conversational. Ready to begin?

**1.** Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft exhale]  
Lately… it’s mostly felt difficult. I’ll catch myself half-smiling if my partner makes a joke, but the laughter just doesn’t bubble up the way it used to. It’s like the baby monitor is always beeping in my head—even when nothing’s wrong—so the funny side of things feels miles away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’m sorry… I’m not sure I understand. Are you asking me to pick one of the choices on the paper, or do you want me to just describe it? If I had to choose, I’d say “not so much lately.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I… I don’t really look forward to much right now. Even the little things I used to enjoy—like my morning coffee or a walk around the block—feel kind of gray. I still do them, but it’s more because I think I should, not because I’m excited.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” I know rationally babies just cry, but I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[sighs and shifts in the chair]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down at night and think, “What if his crib sheet isn’t tight enough and he gets tangled?” Nothing’s actually happened, but the thoughts just pop in and won’t leave until I check on him—again and again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden rush of “something bad is about to happen,” even if everything’s quiet. My heart races and I feel shaky, but there’s no real reason. It usually passes if I pace or do the breathing the nurse showed me, but it’s scary when it hits.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days they do. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to grab sleep in tiny chunks, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I keep lists, but even crossing things off feels heavy—like the next chore is already piling up. I manage, but it’s exhausting.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down and my mind just keeps spinning—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I might’ve done wrong, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. Some nights it takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do, I jolt awake at every little sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do… pretty much every day. It’s like this heavy blanket I can’t shake off. Sometimes I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start leaking out. I try to tell myself it’s just hormones, but the sadness feels deeper than that.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes. It’s happened a few times this week—yesterday I broke down while folding the clean onesies because they looked so tiny and I felt so useless. I try to keep it quiet so my partner won’t worry, but the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[slow head-shake]  
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself.

You've shared how the joy you once found in small pleasures now feels distant and gray, and how every day seems wrapped in a heavy blanket of sadness and self-doubt. Despite working hard to care for your baby, you carry constant worry, nightly tears, and an exhausting sense that you're falling behind. Your honesty about feeling overwhelmed yet still keeping your baby safe highlights both your distress and your strength.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports pervasive loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing even previously enjoyable activities as "gray" and done out of obligation rather than enjoyment, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries about infant safety without cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes that occur "sometimes" and match the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>"Most days they do" and the description of constant strain with tasks piling up aligns with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sleep disruption tied to unhappiness, guilt, and constant worry—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness and spontaneous crying, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying episodes several times this week, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 22 exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>, with high endorsement on core mood, anxiety, and self-blame items that align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Daily <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, and <sym>difficulty concentrating</sym> are present, along with subjective <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym>. Patient denies <sym>self-harm ideation</sym>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Continue to share feelings with trusted family or friends and accept help with household tasks so you can rest
3. Practice short, regular intervals of self-care (shower, 5-minute outdoor step, balanced snack) to bolster energy and reduce stress
4. Arrange practical support for overnight infant care when possible; follow safe-sleep guidelines
5. Begin gentle daily movement such as stroller walks to enhance mood and reduce anxiety
6. Avoid alcohol and limit caffeine; stay hydrated and eat small protein-rich meals to stabilize mood and energy
7. Follow up with provider within one to two weeks; call immediately if thoughts of self-harm develop
8. Contact Postpartum Support International 24-hour warmline at 1-800-944-4773 for peer support and local resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-Equivalent Summary  

**Symptom Endorsement (10/10 items endorsed):**  
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, daily crying spells  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety (health of baby, catastrophic thoughts), with episodic panic symptoms  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia secondary to rumination and hyper-vigilance  
- Overwhelmed / “one step behind,” functional impairment with routine tasks  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (explicit)  

**Pattern / Severity Indicators:**  
- Symptoms present “pretty much every day,” intensity described as “exhausting” and “heavy”  
- Clinically significant distress and role impairment noted  
- No protective psychosocial factors elicited in brief responses  

**Screening Significance:**  
High likelihood of major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, peripartum onset; meets routine cut-off for urgent follow-up assessment.  
Safety: Denies suicidal/homicidal ideation; no acute risk factors identified.  

**Next Step:** Refer for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and evidence-based treatment planning.
